flashcards.q: What is the real modelling difference between RDF triples and a labelled property graph?
flashcards.a: RDF (subject-predicate-object) has no native place to hang properties on a relationship -- qualifying a fact requires reification. Property graphs attach arbitrary key-value properties directly to both nodes AND edges.

flashcards.q: Match each to its query language: RDF, property graph (Neo4j), TinkerPop engines.
flashcards.a: RDF -> SPARQL (W3C standard, declarative). Neo4j -> Cypher (declarative, ASCII-art, basis for ISO GQL). TinkerPop (Neptune, JanusGraph) -> Gremlin (imperative, step-based).

flashcards.q: What is index-free adjacency, and what is its complexity claim?
flashcards.a: Each node stores direct pointers to its adjacent relationships, so a single-hop traversal is a pointer dereference -- O(1) regardless of total graph size -- versus a relational JOIN's cost scaling with table size.

flashcards.q: Name three conditions under which index-free adjacency's O(1) guarantee breaks down.
flashcards.a: Global queries needing a conventional index; supernodes (millions of edges on one node); the graph exceeding available RAM (falls to disk I/O); cross-shard traversal in a distributed graph (network hop per edge crossing a shard).

flashcards.q: Does Amazon Neptune offer a self-hosted deployment option?
flashcards.a: No -- Neptune is fully managed only, unlike Neo4j (self-host or AuraDB) and ArangoDB (self-host or ArangoGraph managed).

flashcards.q: What is ArangoDB's core architectural bet, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: Multi-model: document + graph + full-text/vector search in one engine, one AQL query language -- one operational surface instead of three. Cost: less traversal-specific depth than a specialist graph engine on heavy algorithmic workloads (community detection, centrality at scale).

flashcards.q: Roughly how does Neo4j AuraDB Professional pricing compare to ArangoDB's list pricing?
flashcards.a: AuraDB Professional runs roughly $65/GB/month (Business Critical ~$146/GB/month); ArangoDB is reported roughly 15-25% cheaper list price than Neo4j for comparable deployments.

flashcards.q: What is entity resolution, and why is it consistently under-resourced in knowledge-graph projects?
flashcards.a: Deciding whether records from different sources referring to slightly different representations of the same entity should merge into one node. Under-resourced because teams scope it as a one-time cleanup phase, when it's actually an ongoing pipeline stage that reopens every time a new source system is onboarded.

flashcards.q: What does GraphRAG add over vector-only RAG, and what's the rough indexing cost?
flashcards.a: Extracts entities/relationships into a graph, clusters into communities (Leiden algorithm), pre-summarizes each -- enabling 'global' cross-corpus questions single chunks can't answer. Full Microsoft-style indexing: ~$20-40/million tokens (one-time); LightRAG-style lighter alternative: ~$0.50/million tokens.

flashcards.q: When is GraphRAG NOT worth its indexing cost?
flashcards.a: When real query logs show traffic is dominated by single-document, single-fact lookups -- hybrid search plus reranking captures most of the achievable quality at a fraction of the cost for that majority case.

flashcards.q: What SQL feature replaces most 'we need a graph database' requirements, and what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: A recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) on a well-indexed relational schema handles variable-depth traversal with no new infrastructure, no new query language, and no consistency-model split -- but it degrades at high fan-out or truly unbounded depth compared to a native graph engine.

flashcards.q: What standards body governs RDF, and roughly when was it standardized?
flashcards.a: W3C -- RDF standardized in 2008 (updated 2013), alongside RDFS/OWL for formal ontology and reasoning.

flashcards.q: Why do property graphs handle 'Alice placed Order#42 on 2026-01-04' more naturally than RDF?
flashcards.a: The relationship (PLACED) itself carries the date property directly on the edge. In RDF, a triple has no native slot for qualifying a relationship, so representing the date requires reifying the statement into its own node, multiplying triple count.

flashcards.q: Give a concrete example of a supernode problem and its fix.
flashcards.a: A 'Country: USA' node connected to every US-based user; traversing from it fans out to millions of edges, breaking the O(1)-per-hop assumption. Fix: remodel by bucketing (e.g. by state/region) or invert the query to start from a more selective node.

flashcards.q: Name one genuinely strong use case for a dedicated graph database (not solvable well by a relational CTE).
flashcards.a: Fraud-ring detection: entities are accounts/devices/payment instruments, edges are shared attributes, and the query is 'find densely-connected subgraphs' -- a graph algorithm (community detection/connected-components), not a lookup, which native graph-algorithm libraries (e.g. Neo4j GDS) solve directly.
